Linear nonhomogeneous DE of order n with constant coefficients
Method of undetermined coefficients.

We consider linear nonhomogeneous differential equation of order n with constant coefficients

                     y (n)(x) + a1y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1y ′(x) + any(x) = f (x),                    (1)

where a1, ..., an are real constants and f  is a continuous function on interval I.
We proved that every solution y of the n-th order nonhomogeneous equation (1) can be expressed in
the form
                          y(x) = c1y1(x) + c2y2(x) + ... + cnyn(x) + yp                          (2)

for suitable choice of the constants c1, c2, ..., cn, where yp is a particular solution of linear
nonhomogeneous differential equation (1) and the functions y1, y2, ..., yn are a fundamental set of
solutions of corresponding to (1) linear homogeneous differential equation

                       y (n)(x) + a1y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1y ′(x) + any(x) = 0.                      (3)





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                 3 / 54

A particular solution of DE (1) can be obtained by the method of variation of parameters. But provided
that f (x) is of an appropriate form to construct a particular solution of DE (1) we can use another
method which is called the method of undetermined coefficients. While the method of undetermined
coefficients is not as general as the method of variation of parameters, it is usually much easier to use
when applicable.
I. First consider the case that f (x) is polynomial of degree m

                                         f (x) = b0xm + b1xm−1 + ... + bm−1x + bm,                           (4)

 where b0, b1, ..., bm−1, bm are given constants. Suppose at first that zero is not a root of the
characteristic polynomial (or the characteristic equation) for homogeneous DE (3)

                             λn + a1λn−1 + ... + an−1λ + an = 0.

It is easy to see that then an ̸= 0. In this case it is natural to look for a particular solution of the form

                           yp(x) = A0xm + A1xm−1 + ... + Am−1x + Am.                         (5)





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                 4 / 54

Substituting the function yp in (1), and equating the coefficients of like powers of x, we find from the
terms in xm that anA0 = b0. Since an ̸= 0 we have A0 = b0/an. The constants A1, A2, ..., Am are
determined from the coefficients of the terms xm−1, xm−2, ..., x0.
If zero is a root of the multiplicity s of the characteristic polynomial for homogeneous DE (3), then a
suitable form for yp(x) is

                         yp(x) = xs(A0xm + A1xm−1 + ... + Am−1x + Am).                       (6)

EXAMPLE 1.
Solve DE
                                       y ′′ −y = x2 + 1.                                        (7)


The characteristic equation of the corresponding homogeneous differential equation

                                          y ′′ −y = 0                                           (8)

is
                                         λ2 −1 = 0.

We find the roots
                                      λ1 = 1, λ2 = −1.


Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                 5 / 54

The roots are real and distinct. Thus exp x and exp(−x) are a fundamental set of solutions and the
general solution of corresponding homogeneous DE (8) is

                                 y(x) = c1 exp x + c2 exp(−x),

where c1, c2 are arbitrary constants. Since f (x) is a polynomial of the second degree and zero is not a
root of the characteristic polynomial we look for a particular solution of the form

                                         yp = Ax2 + Bx + C.

On substituting into the original equation we get

                            y p′′ −yp = 2A −Ax2 −Bx −C = x2 + 1.

Equating coefficients of like terms, we have

          −A = 1,  −B = 0,  2A −C = 1 ⇒A = −1,  B = 0,  C = −3.

Hence
                                             yp = −x2 −3

and the general solution of the given DE (7) may be written in the form

Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                 6 / 54

y(x) = c1 exp x + c2 exp(−x) −x2 −3,

 where c1, c2 are arbitrary constants.

Since

we find real roots λ1 = 0, λ2 = 1, and λ3 = −1, what is more the root λ1 = 0 has multiplicity 2. Thus

                                             1, x, exp x, exp(−x)

Putting this into the given equation (9) we have

EXAMPLE 3.
Solve DE
                                        y ′′′ −y ′′ = 2x.                                      (11)

 The characteristic equation of the corresponding homogeneous differential equation

                                         y ′′′ −y ′′ = 0                                       (12)

is
                                        λ3 −λ2 = 0.

Since
                                    λ3 −λ2 = λ2(λ −1),

we find real roots λ1 = 0, λ2 = 1, what is more the root λ1 = 0 has multiplicity 2. Thus

                                                  1, x, exp x

are a fundamental set of solutions for the DE (12) and the general solution of the corresponding
homogeneous DE (12) is
                                  y(x) = c1 + c2x + c3 exp x,

where c1, c2, c3 are arbitrary constants. To find a particular solution we will use two methods.

Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                 9 / 54

Method 1. Method of variation of parameters.
We look for a particular solution of (11) in the form

                               yp(x) = c1(x) + c2(x)x + c3(x) exp x.                           (13)

We suppose that
                                       c′1(x) + c′2(x)x + c′3(x) exp x = 0

and
                                            c′2(x) + c′3(x) exp x = 0.

Then the derivatives of yp take the form

            y p′ = c′1(x) + c′2(x)x + c′3(x) exp x + c2(x) + c3(x) exp x = c2(x) + c3(x) exp x,

                       y p′′ = c′2(x) + c′3(x) exp x + c3(x) exp x = c3(x) exp x.
                                 y p′′′ = c′3(x) exp x + c3(x) exp x.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                10 / 54

Now we substitute y p′′′ and y p′′ into the left-hand side of the equation (11):

                 y p′′′ −y p′′ =  c′3(x) exp x + c3(x) exp x −c3(x) exp x = c′3(x) exp x.

Now to satisfy the equation (11) we require that

                                                c′3(x) exp x = 2x.

Hence, the function yp in (13) is a particular solution of (11) if the functions c′1, c′2, c′3 satisfy the
following system of the equations

                c′1(x) + c′2(x)x + c′3(x) exp x = 0
                                                                  c′2(x) + c′3(x) exp x = 0                             (14)
                                   c′3(x) exp x = 2x.

Method 2. Method of undetermined coefficients.
Since f (x) = 2x is a polynomial of the first degree and the root λ1 = 0 has multiplicity 2, we look for a
particular solution of the form
                                    yp = x2(Ax + B) = Ax3 + Bx2.

Find the derivatives of yp :

                         y p′ = 3Ax2 + 2Bx,   y p′′ = 6Ax + 2B,   y p′′′ = 6A.

Putting this into the given equation (1) we have

                     y p′′′ −y p′′ = 6A −(6Ax + 2B) = −6Ax + (6A −2B) = 2x.

Equating the coefficients of like powers of x, we find

                         −6A = 2,  6A −2B = 0.

Hence
                          A = −1  B = −1.                                             3,

                                                     3

II. As a second case suppose that f (x) is of the form

                                  f (x) = exp(αx)(b0xm + b1xm−1 + ... + bm−1x + bm),                    (15)

 where α, b0, b1, ..., bm−1, bm are given constants. We will call such functions quasi-polynomials. Then
we try to find yp in the form

                      yp(x) = exp(αx)(A0xm + A1xm−1 + ... + Am−1x + Am),                  (16)

provided that α is not a root of the characteristic equation for homogeneous DE (3). If α is a root of the
multiplicity s of the characteristic equation for homogeneous DE (3), then a suitable form for yp(x) is

                     yp(x) = xs exp(αx)(A0xm + A1xm−1 + ... + Am−1x + Am).                 (17)





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                16 / 54

III. Consider the case when f (x) has the following forms

                              f (x) = exp(αx)(b0xm + b1xm−1 + ... + bm−1x + bm) sin(βx)                (26)

or
                             f (x) = exp(αx)(b0xm + b1xm−1 + ... + bm−1x + bm) cos(βx),                (27)

 where α, β, b0, b1, ..., bm−1, bm are given constants. We will call such functions trigonometric
quasi-polynomials. Then a suitable form for yp(x), provided that α + iβ is not a root of the
characteristic equation, is

                  yp(x) = exp(αx)(A0xm + A1xm−1 + ... + Am−1x + Am) sin(βx)+

            + exp(αx)(B0xm + B1xm−1 + ... + Bm−1x + Bm) cos(βx).                 (28)

If α + iβ is a root of the multiplicity s of the characteristic equation for homogeneous DE (3), then a
suitable form for yp(x) is

                 yp(x) = xs exp(αx)(A0xm + A1xm−1 + ... + Am−1x + Am) sin(βx)+

            + xs exp(αx)(B0xm + B1xm−1 + ... + Bm−1x + Bm) cos(βx).                (29)

EXAMPLE 7.
                              y ′′′ −2y ′ + 4y = (x2 + 1) exp x cos x.                           (32)

Determine a suitable form for yp and do not evaluate the constants.
The characteristic equation of the corresponding homogeneous differential equation is

                                      λ3 −2λ + 4 = 0.                                     (33)





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                29 / 54

The equation (33) could have only the following rational roots

                                     ±1, ±2, ±4.

By inspection we find that λ1 = −2 is a root of the equation (33). Dividing polynomial in the left-hand
side of (33) by λ + 2, we obtain

                             λ3 −2λ + 4 = (λ + 2)(λ2 −2λ + 2).

Solving quadratic equation
                                      λ2 −2λ + 2 = 0,

we find conjugate complex roots λ2 = 1 + i and λ3 = 1 −i. Right-hand side of the equation (32) has
the form (27) with α = 1, β = 1. Since α + iβ is a root of the multiplicity 1 of the characteristic
equation (33), a suitable form for yp(x) is

                   yp(x) = x exp x[(Ax2 + Bx + C) sin x + (Dx2 + Ex + F) cos x].





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 21, 2026                30 / 54

EXAMPLE 8.
Solve DE
                              y (4) + y ′′ = 12x + 4x exp x + 2 cos x.                           (34)

 The corresponding homogeneous equation is
